utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom, especially to you, Ms. Lindsay, now on the other side of the room. Due to technical problems with a very important computer, we are sitting in another courtroom today, and we have a delayed start. We will try not to lose too much courtroom time today, so that we should have shorter breaks, only for 20 minutes each, and we will conclude our hearing today, I think, shortly after 2.00 in the afternoon. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please sit down. Good morning, sir. Again, we have a late start --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- and sitting in another courtroom because of technical problems in Courtroom III. Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to greet everybody, and I wish for this trial and this day of trial to end in accordance with God's will, and not my will. I would also like to greet Ms. Lindsay and Mr. Nikolic, and I hope they are going to have a pleasant stay among us here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, yesterday we looked at a document, D64. I would like to have D64 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I think it's not necessary, but I have to remind you again that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies also today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have the document now, "Strictly Confidential," "12th of July," and I told you what it was about briefly because we were in a hurry. The document is about Muslims leaving Srebrenica and crossing the territory controlled by the VRS. They want everybody, including able-bodied men, to cross through those corridors, and at the same time they want to present the situation as if they were attacked by the VRS. And we also ordered that everybody present in the Potocari base was supposed to be registered, and that as large as possible a number of persons should be captured. So this document went to all the corps, including the corps that controlled the territory of the evacuation. We can see that this is a document that contains proposals to the commanders of units whose territories were along the direction of the evacuation of Muslims from Srebrenica. They were supposed to capture them and register them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to tell us whether you knew that this document arrived and whether this document also arrived at your brigade. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, when it's about specific documents, I can talk about them only based on what I see now. In those days, my command and my organ received an endless stream of information and documents. Now I can see this document, and I see that it was addressed to all security/intelligence organs of all the brigades, including my brigade. It arrived on the 12th -- or, rather, it is dated the 12th of July. As far as I can remember, on that day I was duty officer, so that is one more reason to conclude that this document arrived at my brigade, that I saw it, and that I knew its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Did you see that this document contains a proposal to the commanders? Did you, based on this proposal, propose to your commander to register all men that were trying to leave Srebrenica? Thank you. Can we have page 2 in e-court so that the witness could see it. Thank you. The proposal is on the first page, and on the second page, towards the end, under the stamp, it says that it is necessary to register all able-bodied men that are being evacuated from Potocari and the UNPROFOR base there. So did you, in line with this, propose to your commander that they should be registered?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer this question in two parts; first, the part pertaining to all able-bodied men in Potocari that are mentioned in the document, itself. I am sure that I did not propose to my commander to register those persons. Now, as for this sentence under the stamp, that it is necessary to register all able-bodied persons that are being evacuated from the UNPROFOR base in Potocari, this could also have a different meaning. This could relate to another group of people; that is, the able-bodied Muslims who were in the UNPROFOR base and who are technical or other personnel working in the base. There is also another document, another query from my department, that relates to the able-bodied men who were working as technical personnel in the UNPROFOR base. They were all of Muslim ethnicity, they were all Bosniaks, and all the people who worked there were, I think 95 per cent of them, younger persons and able-bodied men. This group, the group that was in the UNPROFOR base, we queried about them, and we received the answer related to them, their registration and their fate. Now, this thing that you are asking me about now, I am almost sure that I did not propose to my commander to register able-bodied men in Potocari and in other locations on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Can we have the first page again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here we have the first page, and we see the fourth paragraph from the bottom, where it says: "Organs for intelligence and security affairs attached to the brigade commands will propose to the commanders of the units positioned along the line of withdrawal of elements of the routed 28th Muslim Division from Srebrenica to undertake all measures to prevent the withdrawal of enemy soldiers and to capture them." And then at the bottom, the last paragraph on this page: "Muslims wish to show that Srebrenica was demilitarised and that it contained only civilian population. That's why they ordered their soldiers to evacuate and move from the area, cross the RS territory, and reach the Muslim-controlled area ..." Do you have any information that other units who were engaged in co-ordinated action with you around Srebrenica registered those persons that they captured on the positions where they were preventing their evacuation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have information that anybody was registering able-bodied men. To be honest, up to this moment I haven't seen any document along that vein, or a document showing that somebody did register people, or a document containing such names of able-bodied men. I haven't seen such a document, and I also haven't heard that anybody else organised this in a planned manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether those who are pulling out from the base in Potocari were registered in some way? Do you know that? Can we have the second page.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in Potocari while the separation was going on, I did not see anybody registering individually people who were being separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see, under the stamp, the following sentence: "It is necessary to register all able-bodied persons who are being evacuated from the UNPROFOR base in Potocari"? Do you see it, and can you tell me, was there any registration of able-bodied men who were leaving the base, because they were all civilians and they were all in the base? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I have to correct you. You know, the fact is that they were not all in the base. A large number of people was outside the base in various other buildings in Potocari. They were temporary accommodation facilities. They were buildings belonging to the former factory. And captured people were all around the place. They were not all in the base. That's simply not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right, thank you. That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you'd permit me just one more thing. I know for sure, because I saw it, because I was there, I know for sure that the people who were being evacuated on the 12th were not in the base. They were in the street, they were close to the base, and they were within the factory perimeter in Potocari, they were in courtyards in Potocari, because it was a large number of people. My estimate is that it was about 30.000 people. They were all gathered there on the 12th before the evacuation. It's a huge number. So I have to express one reservation. Where I was, where I saw the evacuation every time that I arrived there, I never saw that anybody was being registered, that any lists were being made. I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Trial Chamber: These other facilities around the UNPROFOR base, the warehouse, the factory, was it also under the control of the UNPROFOR unit that was stationed there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say what I know for sure, and that is that UNPROFOR controlled the building where it was accommodated. I don't know what exactly you mean when you say "under its control," because if you follow that logic, we could say that it controlled everything within the enclave. However, the actual situation at the time was such that the UNPROFOR forces had their own base that was fenced, physically secure, and I consider this building to be under the control of UNPROFOR. All other buildings were outside this perimeter, and they are not connected in any way -- physically, they cannot connected to the UNPROFOR base. Now, members of UNPROFOR were present there, they were there. However, I saw that the UNPROFOR forces, as they were, and in the numbers in which they were present there, were simply insufficient. Even if they wanted to secure all this, they were not able to secure it. If you want to hear my opinion, I can tell you that all that people, 30.000 of them, could not be physically secured and controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to waste any more time. We don't have much time. You said that you did not see any document relating to the registration.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have D152. It should not be broadcast outside the courtroom because it comes from a protected witness. I would like to take a look at page 3, paragraph 1, and the witness's name should not be revealed. D152. In Serbian and in English, page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see it in the first paragraph: "I knew that it was Mladic because I recognised him, and I was told he would come. I was about 10 to 15 metres from him when he gave a speech, standing by the side of the pitch. He spoke without a megaphone, just normally, as it was very quiet. He stated that he was General Mladic, and said that we would all be exchanged, and that there were hundreds of Serb lines between here and Tuzla, and that not even a bird would be able to get through the lines. He said we would be organised into groups to collect all the bodies from the hills, and then we would be taken to Bratunac to have lunch there. He then chose five of his men to begin making lists of our first and last names, which lasted nearly an hour. One person stood up ..." And so on and so forth, end quote. So, have you seen now the document in which a Prosecution witness, a survivor, describes that there was registration at this particular location? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I don't claim to have the right to comment the statements of other witnesses. This is what this witness said. I'm not disputing it. I'm simply stating what I saw. I'm not disputing it, and I'm not going to comment on it. If you insist that I should comment a statement, then I would have to read the whole statement to see its whole content, because this way you can give me excerpts and segments on the statement which confirm what you are talking about. I can tell you that I have not seen anybody carrying out any planned or organised registration, and I'm being very precise here. I'm talking about taking down the names of the able-bodied men. Now, there were other registrations of a different kind, but while I was in Potocari, there was no registration individually by names of able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Let us not waste any more time about this. You should bear in mind that it may have not been carried out the way that it was proposed to be done in this document. Now, first of all, talking about D64, the document we've seen a moment ago, information distributed to all intelligence/security organs and commands, D64, does it say anything else except the registration and making of lists of people who are leaving the base in Potocari? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, you directed me to certain paragraphs, and I did look at them, but I should not like to make any hasty assessments about whether something else is contained in those documents before I see them in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You directed me to the list or the registration. If you want my opinion, please give me time to see the entire document and I'll tell you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we don't have enough time, I abandon this question. Can we now display D41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, although we have received another list of documents, D152 is not included in these lists; at least in my list. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. I think this is the second time that General Tolimir has referred to not pursuing a certain line of questioning because he claims he doesn't have enough time. Maybe the message didn't get through to him, but I thought the Trial Chamber is pretty clear that we are going to sit a little bit extra today, we are going to take shorter breaks. And from my calculations, from my math, that should provide the accused with more than enough time even to accommodate the additional time that he's been allocated, given the Prosecution's additional time in its examination-in-chief. So I want to disabuse -- or I would ask the Trial Chamber, if the message wasn't received clearly enough, that the accused should be disabused of the idea that he's got to hurry or abandon lines of questioning because he's under some kind of time pressure which, frankly, the Prosecution does not see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was always a condition of the Chamber. Only one small correction. We don't have additional time today, because we started late and we just don't want to lose court time. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Could we now display D41 in e-court for the witness to see. The document was used yesterday as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you saw the document yesterday, tell me -- in your statements, you said you had seen references to the Geneva Conventions somewhere in the document. You said that somewhere in examination-in-chief. In this document -- could we scroll down, please. This is a document from the Main Staff, dated 9 July, and the bottom part says: "In accordance with the order of the president of Republika Srpska, issue an order to all combat units participating in combat around Srebrenica to offer maximum protection and safety to all UNPROFOR members and the civilian Muslim population. Order subordinate units to refrain from destroying civilian targets unless forced to do so by strong enemy resistance. Ban," that is to say "prohibit," "the torching of residential buildings and treat the civilian population and prisoners of war in keeping with the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949." My question is: Did you perhaps see excerpts from this document that was sent to the Drina Corps, to Generals Gvero and Krstic, and references to the Geneva Conventions of 1949?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you are asking me if I saw excerpts related to the Geneva Conventions, or perhaps you're asking whether I saw at the time this document referring to the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us whatever you have seen, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order, this document, I did not see before. I can only assess documents if they had been sent to my organ. Otherwise, there was a huge inflow of documents. Whether I am familiar with Geneva Conventions as a teacher/instructor in Civilian Defence and Protection, I did have some knowledge about what the Geneva Conventions of 1949 imply, without knowing the details, but I can use those documents and I can find my way around them. I can find out how certain issues are regulated by Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Nikolic, did your brigade drive out civilians from their homes and bring them to Potocari, or did they come on their own?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the units of my brigade did not drive out civilians from their homes, for the simple reason that two battalions of my brigade never moved from the lines where they were assigned, whereas one additional battalion was introduced later on a certain axis. I did not have information then, and I do not have information now that anyone, on that route belonging to my brigade, drove out civilians from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: By interviewing those who were able-bodied men who were registered, did you gain information that able-bodied men took the road to Susnjari, whereas women and children headed for Potocari? Did you have such information? Did you work with such information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was kept informed all the time during the combat operations, and I knew that on the route where Serb forces were engaged and that as Serb forces were advancing, everyone else, able-bodied men and civilians, were withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did civilians arrive at Potocari before the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the civilians were already there before the VRS came to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at D002 in e-court. We don't see it yet. It's a document of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, their Main Staff, dated 12 July 1995, where they report the number of Muslim soldiers on the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at line 5 from the bottom: "They organised an attack at Potocari. Around 11.00 p.m., we had 15.000 refugees sitting in the area of combat, together with 300 soldiers of the BH Army on the base in Potocari." Are these the people you mentioned earlier, people who were able-bodied men and who are mentioned in this report by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to their president, Alija Izetbegovic, via the 1st Corps on the 12th of July? Did you have the same information, and did you mean those military-age, able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an intelligence man, I knew that there was a corps - that's what I called it -- a commander of one of their units, one of their brigades, and I knew there were military-aged, able-bodied men in Potocari. However, when I spoke about military-age, able-bodied men, I meant those who arrived together with civilians, those who came to Potocari together with their families, women and children. And in my testimony over the past few days, I believe I once explained a point that I believe to be very important. When I'm talking about military-age, able-bodied men who found themselves among civilians, together with those who came into Potocari, I said, and I can say the same now, that it was my evaluation that a certain number of those people were not militarily engaged. They were able-bodied men, but they were not part of the 28th Division, they were not soldiers. And I am still convinced that a rather large number of men who arrived at Potocari were military age and able-bodied men, but they were not members of the units of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This registration of able-bodied men, and checking their names against the list of those who had committed war crimes, was that all in keeping with rules of warfare and military regulations?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we mean the same thing, General, and that is the so-called triage after a military operation, I am aware that that is in keeping with military regulations and with Geneva Conventions as well. Triage, itself, and separating those who are found to be on the list of suspected war criminals, are not illegal acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. We've had a number of witnesses here who testified that Muslim men were checked against the list of persons suspected of having committed war crimes or any other crimes. One of them was Mr. Kingori, who was a military observer and who testified on the 16th September 2010; page 5509 of the transcript. I asked him: "When you saw that some sort of checking was going on and that Mr. Nikolic was going into a house with a list, did you see him checking against the list of suspects?" And his answer was: "I remember that I spoke about Mr. Nikolic, that he had been to the UNPROFOR base and checked whether some people were to be found on a list." And then comes my question: "Precisely. Did you have access? Did anyone stop you from taking a look at the men who were being checked against those lists?" And then Kingori answers: "Yes. I was there. I was able to see him." He means you: "I was able to see him approaching those men. He would call out a name." And then on page 55 -- I don't know which: "He would approach that man and check him. I think his main purpose was to check whether that person was a soldier or not, because the list was a list of persons whom they knew to be Muslim soldiers." Let me read one more sentence by Kingori, and then I'll put my question. I asked him then: "Did Nikolic single out any man who was under UNPROFOR control after checking him against that list?" And he answered: "If I remember well, I believe there was only one person that he singled out. That one person was injured. That's to the best of my recollection." And on page 5510, lines 1 to 10, he says: "Major Nikolic suspected, based on the list he had, that he was a soldier, and he took him away." That is what all the accusations boil down to, as made by various people against you, Mr. Nikolic. Now, my question is: Do you remember what he is talking about, and do you remember that one person was singled out because their name was found in the list of those who were involved in the war in combat?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember Mr. Kingori, and I know exactly who that person is. We worked together. I think we co-operated well, we worked well together. As for my engagement in inspecting/separating people and having certain lists, what I would like to state here is that I did not have any kind of list in that time that I used. I didn't have any written names or anything like that, in terms of somebody's membership of the 28th Division. I did have in my office, as part of my activities, a record of members of the 28th Division who, according to our information, had committed certain crimes. Amongst them, they were also charged for war crimes. But the list that I had was a list that was not dated on the 12th, nor was it used for that purpose. That list existed from 1992 and was constantly updated. It was not a final list until the end of the -- the fall of the enclave. Even then, it was not a final list. When I handed it over to the Institute for War Crimes in Belgrade, I gave it to Mr. Ivanisevic. I think that Mr. Ivanisevic still has a list of those people. When we're talking about separating people, I know very well in one instance what it's about, and I think that Mr. Kingori made a mistake about the location and the officers who separated that person. We're talking about one member of the Muslim armed forces. I don't know his exact name right now. I have that record in my documents. That person was separated by the State Security Service, and the State Security Service, after separating that person, moved the person to the Zvornik Security Centre and processed him after that. The next person who was separated that I know of, but I think that he was not an active-duty member of the armed forces in Srebrenica, was Mr. -- I will remember his name. He's a politician. Later, he was a deputy in the National Assembly, Ibrahim Mustafic. That's the man who was separated. But, once again, Ibrahim Mustafic was not separated by the army or anybody from the security organ, but he was separated by people from the State Security Service. And I think that Zlatan Celanovic also had a part in this separating of Ibrahim Mustafic. I think that, as far as I know, he recognised him and then they singled him out. What I want to say here, for the sake of the truth, is that one single time when I came to the base, they asked me to check a group of people, and that was when the Dutch Battalion was supposed to leave the base, and the base -- the technical personnel who worked at the base was also supposed to leave together with DutchBat. At the time, I said that we did have a position on that. I knew what our position was, and that those people should leave together with members of DutchBat, and there was no need for me to carry out any kind of check. I saw those people at the base. I didn't make any kind of check, inspection, or did not separate anyone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I please put a short question to the witness just to understand something more precisely. On page 16, lines 18 and the following, you were talking about a list. You said: "I did have in my office, as part of my activities, a record of members of the 28th Division." Could you please tell me who compiled this list, and from whom did you get it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the intelligence/security organ, I was monitoring and recording and investigating crimes that were committed by the 28th Division or by the Muslim side against units -- members of my unit as well as against civilians. For example, in 1992, there was an attack on the village of Kravica. After that attack, as the person who is supposed to deal with that question, I recorded the casualties on the Serbian side, and then I did a classification saying 20 soldiers and 3 civilians were killed. Then later, in my work, by questioning detainees and by gathering other intelligence data from other structures, I learned the names of those who, according to statements, could possibly be the perpetrators of these crimes. If I had any indications that those persons did commit crimes, I would place them on the list of those who could potentially be the perpetrators of a given crime. And then I recorded the combat actions that were carried out on territory under the control of Serbian forces, and where certain crimes were committed, and I did that covering the period practically until the fall of the enclave. I did it according to periods 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, and I did this on the basis of statements, on the basis of gathered information, on the basis of exchanged information, on the basis of information by collaborators, on the basis of information of those who switched sides, fled to the other side with their whole family. Based on all of that information, I placed certain persons on that list, and that was the method that I used to come to that. And Celanovic, Zlatan, this lawyer, was helping me to do this work, and in the bulk of the cases he's the one who did the investigations, who interviewed the witnesses. He helped me in my work. And each time when he interviewed or questioned a certain person, a detainee, somebody who had fled to the other side, if there was a name that was given at such a time, we would place that name on the list of potential perpetrators of crimes. That was the way we worked in my brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that explanation. That means you and some of your colleagues were the authors of this list. You compiled this list according to the information you received during your work; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The list that was in my office was drafted in the way that I described. I know that it turned up -- a list turned up on the 12th. I know that. But that list had the heading of the Bratunac Brigade. The date was the 12th. There was no signature, no stamp, no nothing. And I assert that I did not see that list, and I don't know who drafted it. I know that there was such a list. However, that is not the identical list that I had in my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The list you had in your office was a list you personally compiled; is that correct? That is my understanding of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is a list that I drafted. That was always in my office, and that was handed over -- actually, to be more precise about this, the names of potential perpetrators of crimes were given and informed about to the State Security organs who were doing the same type of work. The final list for that period is with Mr. Ivanisevic at the Institute for War Crimes in Belgrade, because he was the one who was dealing with those matters, he investigated only war crimes, and I felt that it was my responsibility to hand this list over to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please -- Mr. Thayer first.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before we close this sub-chapter and while we're on the topic, I notice that at page 18, line 17, when the witness was describing an attack on Kravica, he referred to a year of 1992. And we've heard a lot of testimony about the attack on Kravica on Orthodox Christmas January 7th of 1993. And just so we have a clear, accurate record, I would just ask if the witness could clarify whether that's a different attack that he was referring to when he said "1992" or whether he misspoke, just so we can have it clear, what he's talking about, and I can maybe save a little time so I don't have to go back on redirect, as long as we're here on the topic. Again, it's at page 18, line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In my view, the answer was very clear, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right. Well, then I'll deal with it in redirect, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, fine. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. I didn't wish to interrupt you while you were talking about this because I felt that you had a need to respond to charges directed at you, and I asked you to talk about this topic. On the 6th of April of this year, the Prosecutor asked you, on page 12401 and 12402, about Mr. Rase [phoen] who was also questioned here by Mr. Celanovic at your office. Can you please tell me if you made any kind of threats against Mr. Celanovic, or did you, in those circumstances, make sure that Mr. Celanovic was treated correctly? Sinanovic, Sinanovic. I apologise, it's Sinanovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I wanted to point out. All that I did in the Sinanovic case, I am now stating here before this Trial Chamber that I would do exactly the same thing in relation to any other prisoner of war. I took him over. He was on the list of potential perpetrators of war crimes specifically relating to the operation in the village of Bjelovac. We had him on our records. I took him over. I brought him to the Bratunac Brigade Command, to the police, handed him over to the authorised person who was authorised by the commander to investigate, to question, to find out if there were any indicia. And I do not see anything there where I made a mistake or should have acted differently. I did what I would have done in any other case, and I would do it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Please, as the security organ, did you also ask your security organs in the brigade and ask Mr. Celanovic, who was authorised by the commander to investigate such crimes, to work professionally, all of you, and did you mistreat anyone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were detained and were brought to my brigade, that I know of, were people that I never saw mistreated in any way. I never permitted any of my people to mistreat any of the prisoners. I wouldn't do it for my own sake, and I believe that the people who were working there were working and doing what they should have been doing, and I think that they were working well. As far as I know, nobody who was brought into my brigade was ever beaten, abused, or mistreated. They were correctly treated. They were interrogated. And for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, the Bratunac Brigade didn't have any kind of detention facility or a prisoner -- prison. We did the best we could. We did question prisoners at the Bratunac Brigade, and after that we would ask the superior command for instructions as to what to do with them. And then we would act pursuant to the orders that came, because, I repeat, there was no prison at the Bratunac Brigade. We would keep the people until they were processed, until they were interrogated, and until we received instructions about what to do with them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Please, can we now look at P1143. Thank you. While we are waiting, I just want to say this was on the 2nd of September, 1992. It's a statement to NIOD, given by Mr. Egbers, who was a witness in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2 of P11143 [as interpreted] - that's an exhibit - so that we can see what he says. This is paragraph 287 on page 27. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You probably know Mr. Egbers. He was an UNPROFOR soldier in Potocari. He states that he also had contacts with each of the sides. 287, thank you. Paragraph 287. Yes, we can see it in the English, and now we're going to see it in the Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps I can help a little bit. This number has three versions of the document; in Dutch, in English, and in Serbian. Now we're seeing it in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, thank you. We can see 287.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Egbers says: "No. But one thing about Nova Kasaba is mentioned. I have it here before me. It says, 'Thursday, 13th of July. At least one of the convoys was stopped at the football field in the surroundings of Nova Kasaba. The BSA set up a place there where able-bodied men were gathered. A number of men were allowed to get in the buses and were transferred to Kladanj.'" Then in paragraph 288, he continues: "Yes. That was another convoy. I was not with it, but I did hear the story that some men were allowed to get in the buses. Maybe they were friends, or acquaintances, or something like that." I am going to put the question to you after Mr. Thayer says what he wants to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we need to be accurate for the record. Paragraph 287 is not Ms. Egbers' words. That is the -- those are the words of the questioner who was putting that as a question to Mr. Egbers. And we went through this when Mr. Egbers came and testified, Mr. President. The italicised text are the questions and the non-italicised text is the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was my observation as well. You see different writing, and one person is asking questions, the other person is answering. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll just wait for the next question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, is it correct that only paragraph 288 is the answer of Mr. Egbers?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Mr. President. I read both the question and the answer. The question is 287, and the answer is 288. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now, please, the question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, did you have information or knowledge that some buses were stopped along the way, that some prisoners were put in the buses, like in this example in Nova Kasaba, and that there were cases of friends putting their friends on the buses and sending them straight to Kasaba? We also saw that at check-points, there were also people who were putting people on the buses, regardless of who they were? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what was going on in the territory of Milici. Kasaba is the territory of Milici, controlled by the Milici Brigade. I can only speak for myself. Yes, I did that, I did help some of my friends. I put them in the bus in Potocari, and everybody knew it. Whether some people in the Milici Brigade were doing the same thing, I wouldn't know. Whether they used to stop buses at the check-points, I also don't know that, and I have no information about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we see the words of Mr. Egbers on the screen, so let us also read paragraph 292, where he says -- 292, can we have that in Serbian as well. It's page 28. Thank you. Where he says the following: "No. Yes. Right. When we stopped by that bus that was burning, you could see also that the Muslims and the Serbs, who had lived together for a number of years before that, still knew each other and were still on friendly terms. They hugged each other. I can very well imagine - it was such chaos - somebody saying, 'These Muslims you just have to stay alive,' stopping a bus and putting these men in it. That's possible." So this is also what Mr. Egbers said. My question is: If you helped some of your friends, do you allow for the possibility that other people at other places, if they had the possibility to do so, also helped some other people, and that's how some people were put on the buses at the check-point in Nova Kasaba? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allow for this possibility, and there is a logical explanation for it. We used to live together, all of us, beginning with me and including all other people. We socialised, we had friends among the Bosnians, we were neighbours, we went to school together, we worked together, we played sports together, and many other things. So it's perfectly normal. I have to emphasise one thing here. Those who did not have any victims, any losses in their families, those whose houses were not set on fire, whose property was not destroyed, those people did not have some additional motive to hate the Bosniaks. I can say for myself that I had friends among the Bosniaks both before the war and after the war. I didn't hate that people, and I still do not hate those people. I'm now speaking about myself, but I do allow for the possibility that there are other people in Kasaba, Milici, and Vlasenica and elsewhere who had friends whom they wanted to help. But in order to avoid any contradiction, yesterday I also said that a large number of people, a large number of families, experienced losses. They lost their children, the members of their families, their property was destroyed, and those people truly felt hatred and intolerance. That's very indicative.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Do you remember that you stated, in the interview conducted by the OTP, that on the first day, there was no separation, and that you spend only about 10 minutes there at that place where the evacuation was being carried out, together with Jankovic, and that after that you left for your unit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember my statements correctly, and I gave a number of statements, I was there at the beginning, when the first convoy was supposed to leave. It is true that in that first convoy, there were some men, and there was no separation in the manner that the separation was carried out later. So I claim what I saw. In the first convoy, men, women, children, complete families were admitted, but that is true only for the first convoy. Later on, they began to separate all the men who tried to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. I just wanted you to confirm what you said and to confirm what Mr. Egbers said. He escorted the convoy from Srebrenica to Tuzla. Can we raise the text so that we can see paragraph 296, where he says: "Yes. But in the beginning, there was no selection. In the beginning, they let everybody in. Only later did they start to select people; on the second day." So Mr. Egbers confirms this. Please, while we are on the subject, I would like to ask you to take a look -- or maybe we don't even have to look at it. Do you remember, is it correct that you separated only about 600 to 650 able-bodied men in Potocari, as opposed to that other huge number mentioned by you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that that's approximately the number. So out of approximately 30.000 people present in Potocari, according to my estimate, then during those two days, 600, 650, or maybe 700 men were separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Now, let us take a look at 65 ter 7280, a Prosecution document, page 11 in Serbian and 11 and 12 in English, line 8 to 13. Here in line 8, you say: "Around 650 during both days." And then the investigator asks you: "Both days?" And you say: "Yes, the 13, or, rather, the 12th and the 13th. The first day, between 300 and 350, the next day between 600 and 650. I'm not sure, but this is the approximate number." Then the investigator says: "Around 650 people in both days?" And you say: "Both days. So the first day, what I just said, and then the next day there was again the process of separation." And then in line 13, he says: "Between 600 and 650." Now that you remember this interview, my question is: Was that the total number of people separated from the mass? Were they handed over to the military police in Bratunac later on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that this is the correct number that I stated earlier. Later on, they were transferred to facilities for temporary detention. And they were secured there, among others, by the military police, but it wasn't only the military police. The civilian police was also engaged in securing this facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this supplement, Mr. Nikolic. Now that we are on the subject, do you remember whether people were brought to you from other locations? Were those people also brought to Bratunac? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, if you are referring to the 12th and the 13th, then my answer is, yes, people were being brought from other locations, and they were also accommodated in those buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move on to the next question: On the 3rd of November, Mr. Baraybar testified here. On the page 7219 of the transcript, lines 18 to 20, he said the minimal number of exhumed bodies from the mass graves was 2.541. In the summary of the testimony of Mr. Baraybar in the Popovic case, the Prosecutor stated that at least 2.541 people were exhumed. It means that he confirmed this number. The exhumations were carried out between 1996 and 2001. So considering this number, that's the number of people exhumed by the International Tribunal, whose representative Mr. Baraybar was, could you tell us whether that's the approximate number of people who were brought to you in Bratunac from various locations? Thank you. Or was it maybe a lesser number?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, I really know nothing about the numbers that you're quoting. I can only say that it was really very difficult to assert the precise number or even an approximate number of people brought to Bratunac. I know where they were accommodated, I know what the situation was like, and I know where, in the town, they were. So besides the facilities I mentioned earlier, the town of Bratunac was full of buses and trucks in all the parking spaces in all the streets, including the parking in front of the municipality building, so it is really very difficult to determine the exact number. We are talking here about a large number of buses and trucks. They were coming in all the time, and people were put up in the facilities that had been designated for that purpose. So I don't know the number. There were many of them. I didn't count them, and I didn't register the people being brought in, and I really cannot answer your question in any precise way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you are testifying here and you are the witness who had most information about the situation in Bratunac, I wanted to ask you because maybe you've discussed the number with the Prosecutor's office. My question is: Bearing in mind what you stated yesterday on page 79, lines 3 to 5, answering the question from Judge Nyambe, and I'm not going to repeat the question because your answer was approximately similar to your present answer, but then you mentioned that your estimate was based: "... also on the count of all the people separated in Potocari and all the people who were detained and brought in Bratunac." So bearing in mind your yesterday's answer and what you just said now, bearing in mind that you also went to Zvornik, do you remember whether that number was larger than the number mentioned by Mr. Baraybar? Was it larger or smaller than 2.541? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only describe what I saw, and maybe that could be the basis for your estimate, just as mine. I wasn't going into details, but let me give you an example. The convoy that left Bratunac on the 14th carrying the prisoners was about two kilometres' long. Mostly, it consisted of buses. So if we look at the transport from the school, then we can see that the convoy was approximately two kilometres' long. Now, how many people could have been in that convoy? Bearing in mind that one convoy left Bratunac towards Drina and Zvornik before that day, then I really don't know what the number could be. Maybe that number is higher, according to my assessment, which means that the total number of persons who left Bratunac could be slightly higher. But I'm really not sure. I am just speculating. I don't know. I told you the size of the convoy, I told you what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have to interrupt you for a moment to correct the transcript. On page 29, lines 22 through 24, you put to the witness the testimony of Mr. Baraybar, and you said: "On the 3rd of November, Mr. Baraybar testified here. On page 7219 of the transcript, lines 18 to 20, he said ..." In fact, that part of the transcript was the summary of the Prosecutor and not the testimony of Mr. Baraybar, just to correct that. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That's quite right, and thank you for correcting the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask the witness: Do you think it's close to that number, 2.541, as Baraybar said? Is that the minimum number? Is that the number you meant in your previous answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said I really don't know the number. But if that's the number determined by experts, I really have no reason to doubt it. I, myself, wouldn't know. I don't want to guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. I don't have any more questions about this. Could we now move to the issue of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you used 65 ter 7280, which is not on the list of documents you wanted to use with the witness. What shall happen with this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This document was on the Prosecution list, and that's why we used it. We thought that once it was proposed by the Prosecution, it may be used by the Defence as well. And we would like to have it admitted, if there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Firstly, Mr. Tolimir, the list -- the purpose of a list of documents to be used during cross-examination is to enable the other party and the Chamber to prepare for the examination. It should be a complete list. Of course, we received long lists of documents of the Prosecution, but if you want to use some of these, you should include them in your list. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just want to note that -- and Mr. Nikolic is no different from a lot of witnesses who have a lot of prior testimony and prior statements. In order for either party to be able properly to cite to a page or put it up on e-court, of course we have to give it a 65 ter number and it needs to be up-loaded in e-court so that we could do that mechanically. That doesn't mean automatically that the Prosecution wants to introduce every single prior statement, transcript of testimony, for every witness for whom it puts these things on its witness list. It's a matter of mechanics, being able to work with these documents, should the need arise. With respect to this transcript, for example, I would just note that it's 130 -- 140 pages in the English and 142 in the B/C/S. I think the accused cited from three or four lines from one page, which the witness confirmed. Again, for us it's, generally speaking, the more the merrier, but, on the other hand, it is a huge document to up-load for the purpose of three or four lines which the witness has confirmed. But I just wanted to make that observation that simply because we have something on our list of exhibits doesn't mean it's something we necessarily want to tender at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. Mr. Tolimir, is it perhaps possible just to tender this page of the document instead of more than 140?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We only started examining on this document. We still have time. If we were to stop here, we could perhaps ask for that page, but we will continue going through that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine. Please continue. Perhaps it's -- I heard your comment. I think it's a good time for our first break, and we will resume at half past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, to move from this subject of prisoners of war on, I would like to take you back to that part of the examination-in-chief where you said that there occurred a disagreement between the civilian authorities and the members of the army at the meeting which you attended about whether the prisoners of war should stay in Bratunac or be moved. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you: Did the representative of the army at that meeting advocate that they should stay in Bratunac, while the civilian authorities wanted them moved to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From what I heard, the civilian authorities wanted the prisoners to be moved to Zvornik from Bratunac, whereas the representative of the army advocated that they should stay in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Was that perhaps influenced by the meeting in Belgrade on the 14th, attended by General Mladic, among others, who insisted that all prisoners of war should be registered and visited by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, I don't see much sense in what you're asking. I really don't know about that meeting in Belgrade on the 14th. I know nothing about it. But all those who were captured in Bratunac had already been moved to Zvornik on the morning of the 14th. The convoy had left on the morning of the 14th. But I really don't know about that meeting in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see D3 in e-court. It's my fault that I didn't show it to you before, Witness. It's a statement of Major General Elliott, secretary to Mr. Carl Bildt. Once we see the document, and it's on the screen now, we'll see the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see it's the statement of Major-General Elliott. It says: "I'm a professional officer of the British Army and hold the rank of major-general." Now, paragraph 2: "On 14 July 1995, I travelled to Belgrade with Mr. Bildt, General De Lapresle (another military adviser to Mr. Bildt) and others. Mr. Bildt attended a meeting with President Slobodan Milosevic of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia between approximately 1300 and 1700 hours. At the conclusion of the meeting, Mr. Bildt debriefed the other members of his delegation, including myself, on issues relating to his meeting with President Milosevic. Later that same evening, at approximately 1900 hours, Mr. Bildt and General De Lapresle met with President Milosevic and General Ratko Mladic, commander of the Main Staff of the Bosnian Serb Army. This meeting concluded at approximately 2200 hours on 14 July 1995." My question: Since this gentleman is referring to that meeting, and you know that meetings are always prepared and planned, do you allow the possibility that Mr. Mladic was informed in advance that this demand would be made and that he had conveyed it to Mr. Beara, and could it be possible that it is because of this that Beara demanded that they should stay in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're asking me to do something that I don't want to go into; namely, speculation, guess-work. You're asking me, Is it possible? Everything is possible, including what you say, but I don't know that. So, yes, it's possible, but I don't know anything about it. I didn't have that information. I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Could we now look at P192, paragraph 17. And that's the statement made by General Rupert Smith to the representatives of NIOD on the 12th of January, 2000. It's P192, paragraph 17. It's D192, paragraph 17. Thank you. Could we see paragraph 17 of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Line 4 from the bottom: "As Mladic said, all this happened quite unexpectedly." This refers to the fall of Srebrenica. The sentence before reads: "The BiH Army fled, and Mladic, with his troops, found himself in the centre of Srebrenica. He was sorry about the death of one Dutch soldier. He was enraged about the air-bomb that nearly missed -- that nearly hit him, and Smith said later, 'I'm sorry I missed you.' Mladic said that men were being captured as prisoners, and Smith said to that that they couldn't all be soldiers. Eventually, Mladic gave permission for the ICRC to visit the prisoners. At the time, he was not concerned about the reports that the BSA had separated men and women in Srebrenica, as the BH Army did exactly the same when they captured large villages. At that time, there was no knowledge of the mass killings." And so on. It says here that Mladic was surprised by the fall of Srebrenica, it was unexpected, and you said the same in your statement. You said the VRS was surprised, taken aback, by the fall of Srebrenica. Is it exact that everyone, including the UNPROFOR, was taken by surprise by the sudden fall of Srebrenica and the gathering of large masses of people in the base in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak in my own name. I, as an officer of the Bratunac Brigade, was surprised by the way in which Srebrenica fell. And later, when talking to other people, other officers, they turned out to share the same opinion. All the prior knowledge and all our prior evaluations about Srebrenica and what is contained in there, the conclusion was that it fell very quickly and with much smaller losses than could be expected, in view of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And then we see the last bit of this paragraph 17: "Eventually, Mladic gave permission for the ICRC to visit the prisoners." Did representatives of the ICRC come to Bratunac following this approval, and did they display any interest in the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know for a fact is that the ICRC came to visit the wounded, but I have no information that the ICRC visited those who were detained in those installations and had the status of prisoners. In other words, I know that the ICRC came to the area of Srebrenica and Bratunac. I know that it was Colonel Jankovic and the physician of the Dutch Battalion who contacted the ICRC, and they were also the ones who supervised the wounded. And I know that it was in the organisation of the ICRC that the wounded were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So they were moved between the 13th and the 14th, and you said the military wanted them to stay in Bratunac and the civilian authorities wanted them moved. Was there anyone at that meeting who said -- who resisted the idea of them staying in Bratunac, who wanted them moved to other locations?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody said they didn't want them registered in Bratunac. It's as I said. Miroslav Deronjic was adamant that they should be moved from Bratunac. That's what I heard with my own ears, and that's what I can testify to. I was saying, in a different context, when they quarrelled, both sides invoked the instructions received from their superiors as to the status of the people detained in Bratunac, but I don't remember hearing anyone opposing a registration of those detained. It's possible that somebody said that, but not in my hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For the record, I must say that we were discussing what was said on transcript page 12416, lines 12 to 14, and 1 to 7, and 46, all the way up to page 12424. When we look at page 12421 to page 12424, I don't want to quote from the transcript, not to waste time. It's a decision -- a meeting that was held on the SDS premises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you help me. Are you referring to the page numbers of another trial? And if so, which one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I asked the question based on the conversation that took place at the headquarters of the SDS, attended by Beara, Lasic and Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it was a very precise question. You gave a page number, and I wanted to know from which document from which case. That's all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm quoting transcript from the examination-in-chief of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly request that the microphone be pushed a bit to the right, the left-hand microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, the Prosecutor asked you about 65 ter 728. The Prosecutor asked you whether you were conveying information first to the security organs and only then to your commander, and you said that you would always inform your commander first, and that you never informed the security organs first and your commander only later. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have just mentioned 65 ter 728. I think that was a mistake. Perhaps you were referring to 65 ter 7280. I have no idea. Look on the screen. There is a certain document. I don't know if that is the right one. Please check the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. You're right, 7280, yes, 7280. I also noticed that something was amiss.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, was there a general principle in force in security/intelligence organs that they should inform first their immediate superiors, their commanders, and then after that the appropriate commands? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, as far as all the rules of service and the relationship you just mentioned, I can answer in the affirmative. I can tell you that in almost all cases, when my commander was in the brigade, when he was present there, when he was available for me, all the reports and everything I had to tell him during the day, I would first give to my commander in my brigade. And then after that, all the information I considered relevant I would include in my written daily reports which were sent to the intelligence/security organ of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now let us take a look at 7280, page 15 in Serbian and 16 in English, lines 11, 12 and 13. That's where you say that. I didn't read it out aloud on purpose, because I wanted you to give your answer without it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So lines 11, 12 and 13: "Q. Was there ever a situation that you skipped informing the commander and went straight to security/intelligence organs in the corps or the Main Staff ..." And then you answered: "No, I did not do that." And that's exactly what you just said. So based on all this, my question is: Did you maybe get the impression, during the investigation and during the trial, that everybody wanted to think that you had some superiors outside of the brigade and that your superiors were not organs of the command of the brigade? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say, based on my own experience during that period, is approximately as follows: There was some misunderstanding about who commanded the security/intelligence organs, also a misunderstanding about to whom they reported, and there was one more misunderstanding or lack of understanding related to command and control, on one side, and professional control or directing of units. People didn't quite know things in those areas, and of course I tried to explain these issues, within my abilities, the relations between me and my commander, the relations between me and my immediate superior professional organ, our duties and our competences in that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we are going to move to another subject. This same document, 7280, page 17 in English and 16 in Serbian, lines 23 to 26. Thank you. I quote from line 23 - maybe you can see it too - where you say: "I was informed that on the evening on the 11th, there was going to be a meeting in the Fontana Hotel. For the first time, I heard about this meeting from Colonel Jankovic. We were told then that the meeting was going to be between General Mladic and the representatives of the Dutch Battalion." Do you remember this first meeting, held in the evening on the 11th of July? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 19 in Serbian of this same document, page 22 in English, lines 15 and 16, you were asked: "Did you know that your commander, Blagojevic -- did you know where your commander was when you left the brigade? "A. I didn't. "Q. Was he present, and did he have command within the zone of his responsibility on the 11th of July? "A. Yes, he was present." Now we have to clarify this. Do they think -- do they intend to ask whether that he was present at the meeting or whether he was present in the zone of responsibility of the brigade? Could you clarify this for the record?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the question was about Colonel Blagojevic being present in the zone of responsibility of the brigade. That's what I thought at the time, and I still think so. And I answered, yes, he was present in the zone of responsibility of the brigade. As far as I know, Colonel Blagojevic was not in Fontana, he did not attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to clarify this before we moved on. Now, can we take a look at P591. That's a video or, rather, the Srebrenica video. It lasts for 46 minutes, and we are going to see that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "What do you want? "I've been asked for a meeting --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the video to be stopped at 46:32.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you hear the first sentence, where they say General Mladic -- where General Mladic says: "You wanted to have the meeting. What do you want?"

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: This meeting on the evening of the 11th, was it requested by Karremans or by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, I don't know who requested the meeting. I was only informed by Colonel Jankovic what I was supposed to do about the meeting. But who asked it -- who asked for it, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. But did you hear it now in the video that it was Karremans who asked for the meeting? Can we play this segment again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "What do you want?" "I've been asked for the meeting. I had a talk with General Nicolai two hours ago, and also with the national authorities, about the request on behalf of the population. It's a request, because I'm not in a position to demand anything."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We stopped at 47:18.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you hear now that Colonel Karremans says that he spoke to General Nicolai in Sarajevo and also with the representative of the civilian population, and that he speaks in their name, and that he requests those things in their name because he's not authorised to demand anything?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard what it is possible to hear in this video.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have the sound.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "... and that I've been ordered by BH Command to take care of all the refugees, and are now approximately 10.000 women and children within the compound of Potocari. And the request of the BH Command is to -- let's say, to negotiate or ask for the withdrawal of the battalion and withdrawal of those refugees, and if there are possibilities to assist that withdrawal. There are some women who are able to --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We stopped at 48:34.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you hear Karremans say, and the interpreter interpret, that he had received an order from the UNPROFOR Command in Sarajevo to negotiate about the evacuation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see this video from 48:34 further on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "And what I've heard from all those soldiers who are now working to -- let's say, to ease the pain for the population ... a lot of people -- a lot of persons, women, said, 'We are waiting for the buses and can we leave the enclave,' because they are sick, tired, they are very scared --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we stop. We stopped at 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you hear when Karremans said that the population was waiting for the buses so that they could leave the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on from 49:05. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "And I've been asked by General Nicolai -- asked for, let's say, for a kind of humanitarian assistance, like food and medicines, because even in my battalion I don't have fuel, almost nothing, fuel left, because of the rejection of all the clearances of the last four months. We have been --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your conversation with the Prosecutor, you said that you were present at all three meetings held in Fontana. You said that you secured all the three meetings with the police forces, and that you were in another room, but that the door between the larger and the smaller room was open. Is that so? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, you said something probably by accident. You said that I was present at all three meetings and that I had declared that before. If you're talking about the organisation of the three meeting, then I would agree with you. I was present during the preparations for the three meetings, and I secured the participants of all three meetings. However, during the first two meetings, I was inside Fontana, inside the building, while during the third meeting I was not inside with the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, that's exactly what you said, but I wanted to avoid quoting all the pages. Now, since you were present at the first meeting, tell the Trial Chamber at whose initiative the first meeting was held. Was it the initiative of General Mladic or Karremans? And who was it who demanded the evacuation of the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have asked this question some minutes ago. You received the answer. The witness didn't know. He just was only able to confirm what he heard in the video. Please, no repetitions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. On the basis of the video, and since he said that he was present during the first meeting, I'm asking you -- I'm asking him if he knows, since he was present, who requested the meeting, Was it Mladic or somebody else? I leave it in your hands. If you believe that this question is not important, then I will move to another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you misunderstood. You put the question several minutes ago to the witness, and he said he didn't know. That's all. Please, don't put this question a third or a fourth time, and continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, I stopped the video and asked you whether you heard, whether you heard, whether you heard. Now, based on the entire video, could you please tell us who asked for the evacuation of civilians from Potocari? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, sir, you are insisting on an answer. I just want to be precise. After -- or looking at this video footage and reminding myself of the events that are recorded here, I can completely answer your question that the meeting was initiated by Mr. Karremans, the DutchBat commander, and I can say that after looking at the video, but I want to be very precise. I didn't know that when I got the assignment to secure the Fontana, and I didn't go it, I didn't pay attention to particulars. I did observe what was going on, but I didn't pay attention to who requested the meeting and things like that. After looking and listening to the footage, I can say that it was Mr. Karremans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to put a correction on the record. This document is not P591, but P991, the trial video. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, can you please tell us when the second meeting at the Fontana Hotel was held? Why was it held, and at whose initiative?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second meeting at the Fontana was held on that same evening at about 2200 hours, 2215 hours. I don't know the precise time, but it was approximately then. And I think it was held at the request of General Mladic, who insisted that they bring representatives of the 28th Division of the Muslim army to the meeting. That's what I heard, after the first meeting and the request by General Mladic to return that same evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And were you there that same evening on the 11th, at the second meeting held at the request of General Mladic, who requested representatives of the Muslim army? Do you know what happened at that meeting, what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the Hotel Fontana. I know that at the second meeting, that evening the Serbian side was present, General Mladic, and a group of officers with him. It was also attended by representatives of DutchBat, the commander and his associates. There was also a representative of the Muslim side. I think his name was Nesib Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the representatives of the Muslim side requested at the meeting between the UNPROFOR, Mladic and them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the details from the meeting. Generally, what I remember is that there was discussion about their status, the fate of those people, their possible evacuation, and the issue of fuel and problems relating to the overall situation in Potocari. I think that one of the requests was, and that was something that General Mladic insisted on in particular, that the Muslim army had to surrender, lay down their weapons. So other than the question of the status of those in Potocari, there was also emphasis on this second issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a third meeting held the following day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The third meeting was held the following day, the 12th, also at the Fontana.
